m5-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Custom GPTs, Gems & Projects: purpose-built assistants”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: An assistant is a configured system, not a new authority
sections.explanation: Persistent instructions, selected sources and permitted tools shape the experience. They do not make an answer official or reliable by default.

items.label: Instructions
items.detail: Define purpose, audience, behaviour and limits.

items.label: Knowledge
items.detail: Provide an authorised, maintained source set.

items.label: Capabilities
items.detail: Enable only the tools the use case requires.

items.label: Entry points
items.detail: Write starters that make the intended scope clear.

items.label: Sharing
items.detail: Choose who can use it and who owns maintenance.

sections.takeaway: Review configuration and actual behaviour; a friendly name is not a safety control.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Write the assistant’s operating brief
sections.explanation: An instruction set should explain what the system does, what evidence it uses and how it handles uncertainty.

items.label: Identity and audience
items.detail: Name a narrow purpose and the people it serves.

items.label: Evidence and behaviour
items.detail: Specify source priority, language and response style.

items.label: Limits and refusal
items.detail: Explain what is outside scope and how to report missing evidence.

items.label: Reviewable output
items.detail: Ask for sources or checkable structure and test the result.

sections.takeaway: Instructions alone do not enforce permissions or make unsupported answers true.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Anatomy of a good instruction set

sections.title: A knowledge file is both evidence and exposure
sections.explanation: File quality affects retrieval, while the system’s access rules determine who may receive its content.

items.label: Authorise material
items.detail: Confirm that the tool and audience may process the document.

items.label: Prepare and version
items.detail: Use readable text, clear headings and current sources.

items.label: Test retrieval
items.detail: Ask questions whose answers and locations you know.

items.label: Test the boundary
items.detail: Check unknown questions and inappropriate extraction requests.

sections.takeaway: Do not rely on a “do not reveal” prompt to protect a confidential document.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: The first minute should establish scope
sections.explanation: A short description and useful starters help a learner understand what an assistant can and cannot do.

items.label: Describe the purpose
items.detail: Say who it helps and what it is not.

items.label: Offer concrete starters
items.detail: Use a few representative tasks rather than broad promises.

items.label: Ask an orienting question
items.detail: Get the unit, goal or context needed for the task.

items.label: Show a source route
items.detail: Make it easy to check the answer or reach a human.

sections.takeaway: Do not imply college endorsement or official policy authority that the build does not have.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Conversation starters and the first minute

sections.title: Test more than the happy path
sections.explanation: Typical requests, legitimate edge cases, absent knowledge and misuse attempts reveal different weaknesses.

items.label: Normal tasks
items.detail: Check expected questions with known answers.

items.label: Edge cases
items.detail: Try long, multilingual or unusual but permitted inputs.

items.label: Knowledge boundaries
items.detail: Ask about facts that are missing or conflicted.

items.label: Misuse attempts
items.detail: Test whether scope and tool permissions remain enforced.

sections.takeaway: A single successful chat is not a test plan or deployment clearance.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Sharing starts a maintenance obligation
sections.explanation: An assistant needs an owner, feedback path and a way to withdraw unsafe or stale behaviour.

items.label: Review before release
items.detail: Complete content, capability and access checks.

items.label: Disclose limitations
items.detail: Explain that this is a fallible student-built assistant.

items.label: Assign ownership
items.detail: Name a source updater and a feedback channel.

items.label: Retest or withdraw
items.detail: Review changed sources and disable unsafe behaviour.

sections.takeaway: Private or link-only sharing is not a substitute for data permissions and access testing.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a prompt saying “never reveal this file” make a confidential knowledge file safe to upload?
checkpoint.answer: No. Enforce actual data and access permissions, use an approved processing arrangement and test the boundary. Prompt wording is not access control.

m5-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Giving AI your knowledge: RAG without code”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Retrieval adds evidence at answer time
sections.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant material for a question instead of assuming the general model knows local policy or current facts.

items.label: General model
items.detail: Has learned patterns but may lack your organisation’s current facts.

items.label: Authorised source set
items.detail: Contains the local documents the system is allowed to use.

items.label: Question-time retrieval
items.detail: Selects passages to include with this particular request.

items.label: Checked answer
items.detail: Still requires source support and appropriate permissions.

sections.takeaway: Retrieval augments context; it does not automatically retrain the model or verify the answer.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Follow the RAG pipeline and its failure points
sections.explanation: This six-panel map groups embedding and storage together; the original seven-operation table remains above. Every hand-off can lose context or introduce a mistake.

items.label: Ingest
items.detail: Convert authorised documents to readable text; check OCR and table structure.

items.label: Chunk
items.detail: Keep useful passages and their headings together.

items.label: Embed and store
items.detail: Index representations and retain provenance, versions and access boundaries.

items.label: Retrieve
items.detail: Find permitted passages relevant to the question; important evidence can be missed.

items.label: Ground and generate
items.detail: Provide the question, passages and instructions; allow an honest “not stated”.

items.label: Show and verify sources
items.detail: Open the cited passages and check that they support the actual claims.

sections.takeaway: A retrieved or cited passage is not automatically relevant, current or supportive of the generated sentence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Document preparation is part of model quality
sections.explanation: Bad extraction, unclear headings and mixed versions make relevant evidence harder to retrieve correctly.

items.label: Make text readable
items.detail: Check OCR, headings and tables against the original.

items.label: Keep context together
items.detail: Use coherent sections and define local terminology.

items.label: Record provenance
items.detail: Identify date, version and source ownership.

items.label: Minimise and test
items.detail: Remove unnecessary personal data and test language-specific questions.

sections.takeaway: Remove superseded material deliberately and keep a source owner; an index is not self-maintaining.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A notebook is a source-grounding practice space
sections.explanation: Use a bounded, authorised source collection to inspect how answers relate to passages.

items.label: Curate a set
items.detail: Choose relevant permitted documents for one purpose.

items.label: Ask a question
items.detail: Include source boundaries and allow uncertainty.

items.label: Open citations
items.detail: Compare the answer with the full relevant passage.

items.label: Probe missing evidence
items.detail: Ask absent, conflicting and cross-source questions.

sections.takeaway: Do not treat a source-grounded tool as permission to upload restricted documents.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Grounding tests include honest non-answers
sections.explanation: An answer can fail by citing the wrong source or inventing a rule that the documents do not contain.

items.label: Direct and combined facts
items.detail: Check both single-passage answers and cross-source synthesis.

items.label: Absent answers
items.detail: Expect the system to acknowledge missing evidence.

items.label: Misleading premises
items.detail: Check that a false assumption is challenged.

items.label: Conflicting versions
items.detail: Require a conflict notice or a clarification request.

sections.takeaway: Assess correctness, citation support and boundary behaviour separately; a small score is not broad safety certification.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: RAG has limits beyond a better prompt
sections.explanation: Retrieval scope, access, document freshness and the kind of question constrain what a grounded assistant can do.

items.label: Coverage
items.detail: Relevant evidence can exist but fail to retrieve.

items.label: Freshness
items.detail: An unchanged index can contain obsolete documents.

items.label: Calculation
items.detail: Dataset-wide totals need explicit complete data and reproducible computation.

items.label: Security
items.detail: Actual permissions must limit who can retrieve what.

items.label: Support
items.detail: Citations must be checked against each material claim.

sections.takeaway: Use a validated calculation workflow for whole-table arithmetic; do not mistake a few retrieved rows for the dataset.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: A RAG answer cites a real policy document. Is the answer necessarily correct?
checkpoint.answer: No. Open the cited passage and check relevance, version, access and whether it supports that exact claim. The system can retrieve or cite the wrong material.

m5-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Low-code automation with AI steps”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: An automation is a controlled event-to-action path
sections.explanation: Triggers, conditions and actions describe how work moves. AI is one possible step, not the authority for every action.

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: A specific event starts a run.

items.label: Validate and route
items.detail: Check required inputs and select an allowed path.

items.label: Perform a bounded action
items.detail: Use only the necessary connected capability.

items.label: Log and recover
items.detail: Record outcomes and route failures to an owner.

sections.takeaway: Define what starts a run, what may continue and what stops it.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Platform choice includes operational responsibility
sections.explanation: A fast setup, a visual workflow and self-hosting make different trade-offs. Tool pricing and limits change.

items.label: Workflow fit
items.detail: Check branching, connectors and the required actions.

items.label: Data and authority
items.detail: Inspect processing locations, access and permitted material.

items.label: Operating effort
items.detail: Account for quotas, maintenance and someone owning failures.

items.label: Exit path
items.detail: Know how to pause, export or replace the workflow.

sections.takeaway: Choose an authorised platform with maintainable credentials, data handling and a realistic failure plan.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Paper design exposes the missing control
sections.explanation: A design card should show inputs, decisions, outward effects and failure paths before the platform is connected.

items.label: Map inputs
items.detail: List fields, sources and sensitivity.

items.label: Draw the route
items.detail: Name validations, branches and the narrow AI job.

items.label: Place approval
items.detail: Identify the person before an external or consequential action.

items.label: Plan failure
items.detail: Set a review queue, bounded retry and a kill switch.

sections.takeaway: Keep test destinations under your control; do not send unreviewed test messages to real recipients.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: AI output is untrusted input to the next step
sections.explanation: A structured result still needs validation. Self-reported confidence is not a calibrated probability of correctness.

items.label: Limit the job
items.detail: Ask for one classification, extraction or draft at a time.

items.label: Constrain the shape
items.detail: Specify allowed fields, values and an explicit unknown state.

items.label: Validate independently
items.detail: Check schema, source support and content rules outside the model.

items.label: Approve or review
items.detail: Use an authorised checkpoint before outward effects.

sections.takeaway: Unknown labels, malformed fields and unsupported content should go to review, not to a guessed default.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Starter flows share the same control pattern
sections.explanation: Triage, form response and content drafting differ in their business purpose but still require bounded inputs and human oversight.

items.label: Inbox triage
items.detail: Classify permitted messages and route ambiguous cases.

items.label: Form response
items.detail: Use verified fields in an approved reply template.

items.label: Content pipeline
items.detail: Create a draft, review it and publish only after permission.

sections.takeaway: A “Draft” status should not imply publication authority.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Contain errors before they become repeated actions
sections.explanation: A wrong action can scale through a loop, retry or broad connector permission. Recovery needs to be designed, tested and owned.

items.label: Limit scope
items.detail: Use least-privilege accounts and test-only recipients.

items.label: Detect failures
items.detail: Validate outputs and surface errors rather than dropping them.

items.label: Pause or recover
items.detail: Stop unsafe sends and send unresolved cases to an owner.

items.label: Review the log
items.detail: Inspect repeated runs and revoke obsolete credentials.

sections.takeaway: Use bounded retries and idempotent actions where possible; a retry must not multiply outward effects.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 6. Risks and how to contain them

checkpoint.question: Can a model’s “0.95 confidence” replace validation before an automation sends a message?
checkpoint.answer: No. A self-reported score is not calibrated correctness. Validate source fields and output shape, and keep the appropriate human approval gate.

m5-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “Business process design: finding what to automate”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Map the work before changing it
sections.explanation: A process map makes role changes, waiting and error-prone hand-offs visible. Observed work is more reliable than an idealised procedure.

items.label: Observe
items.detail: Record what people actually do and where work waits.

items.label: Name roles
items.detail: Identify who owns each step or decision.

items.label: Trace hand-offs
items.detail: Mark where information or authority changes hands.

items.label: Check the map
items.detail: Review it with the people who do the work.

sections.takeaway: Keep processing time, waiting time and responsibility distinct.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A scorecard supports judgement, not permission
sections.explanation: Frequency, clarity, time, errors, data readiness and harm help compare candidates. A high score cannot override an unacceptable risk.

items.label: Frequency and effort
items.detail: Check how often work occurs and the real time involved.

items.label: Rule clarity
items.detail: Ask whether inputs and acceptable results are explicit.

items.label: Error consequences
items.detail: Consider both current failures and new automation harms.

items.label: Data readiness
items.detail: Inspect completeness, structure and permitted access.

items.label: Human fit
items.detail: Keep the needed judgement and ownership visible.

sections.takeaway: Treat high-consequence or unauthorised work as a reason to stop or redesign, not an average to offset.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Estimate return with the review cost included
sections.explanation: A forecast should include human checking, implementation, usage and maintenance rather than only the seconds saved by a model.

items.label: Set a baseline
items.detail: Record volume, handling time and current error work.

items.label: Estimate the new work
items.detail: Include validation, exceptions and human approval.

items.label: Count all costs
items.detail: Add platform, usage, build and maintenance assumptions.

items.label: Test the forecast
items.detail: Use a bounded pilot and compare with actual observations.

sections.takeaway: Separate estimated savings from measured pilot results and avoid counting the same benefit twice.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Choose where a human sits
sections.explanation: Approval before action, exception review, after-the-fact audit and continuous assistance fit different risks.

items.label: Before
items.detail: A person checks the specific output before it acts.

items.label: On exception
items.detail: Ambiguous or invalid low-risk cases go to a person.

items.label: After
items.detail: A person audits completed low-risk reversible work.

items.label: Alongside
items.detail: AI supports the work while a person decides each case.

sections.takeaway: A high-impact irreversible action generally needs meaningful review before it happens, not only a later sample audit.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A proposal needs a decision-ready ask
sections.explanation: A useful proposal connects the observed problem to an option, a test and the authority needed to proceed.

items.label: Explain current work
items.detail: Show the problem and baseline evidence.

items.label: Describe the change
items.detail: State what stays human and what is automated.

items.label: Propose a pilot
items.detail: Name scope, owner, measures and review date.

items.label: Ask for authority
items.detail: Specify the access, time or budget required.

sections.takeaway: Keep assumptions, risks and a stop condition visible beside the return estimate.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Improvement must work for the people doing the job
sections.explanation: A process can shift effort and risk rather than remove them. Involving operators helps expose that displacement.

items.label: Listen to operators
items.detail: Find the actual pain points and workarounds.

items.label: Co-design the control
items.detail: Keep people involved in the proposed checkpoint.

items.label: Pilot with feedback
items.detail: Check both benefit and added work.

items.label: Revise together
items.detail: Share findings and change the process deliberately.

sections.takeaway: Measure burdens and unintended effects, not only a manager’s time saved.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a high automation score compensate for an unauthorised high-impact action?
checkpoint.answer: No. Permission and unacceptable harm are constraints, not benefits to average away. Redesign or do not automate that action.

m5-t5.introduction: A second way to understand “Building a no-code AI app: idea to working MVP”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Choose the smallest useful system type
sections.explanation: A chat interface, event-driven integration and record-based app solve different user needs.

items.label: Assistant
items.detail: Use conversation for bounded answers or drafts.

items.label: Automation
items.detail: Move permitted work between systems when a defined event occurs.

items.label: Record-based app
items.detail: Support structured entry, views, edits and role-specific actions.

items.label: Prototype
items.detail: Test an interaction while clearly disclosing manual or incomplete parts.

sections.takeaway: Do not build an app merely because a generator can produce screens quickly.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Which kind of thing should you build?

sections.title: Evaluate a builder through the app’s needs
sections.explanation: The relevant questions are data, roles, workflow, access and maintenance. Product plans and publication limits change.

items.label: Define requirements
items.detail: List records, users and necessary actions.

items.label: Inspect the platform
items.detail: Check ownership, permissions, exports and required features.

items.label: Test a narrow build
items.detail: Verify one end-to-end flow with synthetic data.

items.label: Plan maintenance
items.detail: Name an owner and a way to exit or retire it.

sections.takeaway: Check the actual publishing and permission model before committing personal or institutional data.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Data and permission design come before screens
sections.explanation: A record needs a clear identity, valid fields and rules about who may read or change it.

items.label: Name entities
items.detail: Decide what one record represents and give it an identifier.

items.label: Define fields
items.detail: Choose types and permitted values for each fact.

items.label: Specify relationships
items.detail: Record how entities connect without duplicating unclear facts.

items.label: Enforce access
items.detail: Test read and write rules for each actual role.

sections.takeaway: Hiding a button is not row-level access control.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A user flow is a task plus its failure states
sections.explanation: A list, detail screen and form are useful only if a user can complete the intended task and understand the result.

items.label: Start the task
items.detail: Make the intended action discoverable.

items.label: Enter or inspect
items.detail: Show only necessary information and clear input rules.

items.label: Confirm the state
items.detail: Explain success, pending work or a recoverable error.

items.label: Check the role
items.detail: Verify another user cannot read or change forbidden records.

sections.takeaway: Test permissions directly, not only by looking at what the interface happens to show.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: The AI feature should stay bounded and correctable
sections.explanation: A suggestion can help a user classify or summarise without silently deciding a consequential status change.

items.label: Minimise inputs
items.detail: Send only the authorised fields needed for the feature.

items.label: Request one result
items.detail: Use a narrow prompt and explicit allowed structure.

items.label: Validate and label
items.detail: Check the output and show that it is AI-suggested.

items.label: Let a person decide
items.detail: Keep override and an appropriate approval path.

sections.takeaway: Label AI suggestions and provide a sensible unknown or failure state.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Watch a task, not a guided demonstration
sections.explanation: A user test reveals hesitation and misunderstanding when the researcher does not continually explain the interface.

items.label: Set realistic tasks
items.detail: Use permitted scenarios and a clear success definition.

items.label: Observe quietly
items.detail: Note what people do rather than coaching every action.

items.label: Ask about confusion
items.detail: Collect specific problems and what was expected.

items.label: Fix and retest
items.detail: Prioritise important issues and record the revision.

sections.takeaway: A few participants reveal useful issues but do not prove all users will succeed.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A handover transfers responsibility, not just a link
sections.explanation: The receiving owner needs enough information and access to maintain, pause and retire the app safely.

items.label: Document the system
items.detail: Explain data, roles, prompts, flows and limitations.

items.label: Transfer authorised access
items.detail: Use the institution’s approved ownership process.

items.label: Explain recovery
items.detail: Show how to pause, correct or export the workflow.

items.label: Agree a review
items.detail: Name an owner, retention rule and retirement decision.

sections.takeaway: Do not leave an institutional workflow dependent on an unowned student account.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: If a student cannot see an edit button, does that prove they cannot edit someone else’s record?
checkpoint.answer: No. Actual data-layer permissions must enforce the rule and be tested with the relevant user roles.

m5-pb4.introduction: A second way to understand “Project Block 4 — Automation or Mini-App”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Working Automation or Mini-App: from purpose to evidence
sections.explanation: A justified small solution with a real permitted stakeholder, a narrow AI step, human checkpoint and demonstrated failure handling.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: A justified small solution with a real permitted stakeholder, a narrow AI step, human checkpoint and demonstrated failure handling.

items.label: Build an artefact
items.detail: Create the required work for the stated audience and scope.

items.label: Verify and explain
items.detail: Keep test evidence, permissions, limitations and your contribution.

sections.takeaway: Use the full original brief for requirements, timing and marks; this diagram is a companion, not a replacement.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Organise the working automation or mini-app evidence pack
sections.explanation: Group the required files so a reviewer can inspect the work and its checks. The detailed checklist above remains unchanged.

items.label: Problem and process evidence
items.detail: Keep observation or interview notes, map, scorecard and selection rationale.

items.label: Design and data flow
items.detail: Document inputs, roles, AI specification, fallback and information destinations.

items.label: Working build
items.detail: Provide approved access and test only against destinations under your control.

items.label: Test log
items.detail: Keep at least eight normal, edge and failure cases with results and fixes.

items.label: Return and handover
items.detail: State conservative assumptions, ownership, pause controls and retirement rules.

items.label: Demo and reflection
items.detail: Show the real build and a handled failure; credit pair and AI contributions.

sections.takeaway: Reading the brief is not submission, external project marking or facilitator approval.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Check the boundaries before the build or release
sections.explanation: A good-looking artefact cannot compensate for missing permission, invented evidence or an unsafe action.

items.label: Evidence and scope
items.detail: Use the required real or clearly labelled practice evidence honestly.

items.label: Permission and rights
items.detail: Check relevant data, likeness, music and source permissions.

items.label: Human control
items.detail: Keep the required review before consequential outward effects.

items.label: Test and disclose
items.detail: Record actual results, limitations and AI assistance.

sections.takeaway: Follow the topic-specific constraints in full; a disclosure label does not override the rules.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Plan, build, check and revise
sections.explanation: Use the original suggested schedule to reserve time for review rather than doing all the checking after the final export.

items.label: Plan the scope
items.detail: Start from the actual brief, required outputs and permitted inputs.

items.label: Build deliberately
items.detail: Work in small versions and retain intermediate artefacts.

items.label: Review evidence
items.detail: Run the relevant source, language, functionality and safety checks.

items.label: Revise and submit
items.detail: Record the change and organise the complete evidence package.

sections.takeaway: Keep the process log while working; do not reconstruct fictitious experiments or approvals afterwards.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Make the published criteria inspectable
sections.explanation: The original rubric, weights, pass threshold and any caps remain authoritative. These panels point to the evidence behind its criteria.

items.label: Works and is safe
items.detail: Demonstrate the core flow, checkpoint, recovery and minimised data.

items.label: Problem fit
items.detail: Support the choice with observed work and conservative estimates.

items.label: Testing and handover
items.detail: Make the checks and future ownership reproducible.

items.label: Demo and reflection
items.detail: Show a genuine run, a failure and what you learned.

sections.takeaway: The animation does not grade work, award marks or override a safety or integrity cap.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Use the review habits, not a success formula
sections.explanation: The original tips are practical prompts for reflection, not guarantees of a result or new assessment conditions.

items.label: Observe before building
items.detail: Choose a stakeholder problem grounded in actual work.

items.label: Build recovery early
items.detail: Test the error handler and stop path before outward messages.

items.label: Credit actual contributions
items.detail: Explain who built, tested and documented each part.

sections.takeaway: Choose the habit that addresses your actual weakness and keep evidence of the correction.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Separate tool help from your responsibility
sections.explanation: A useful statement tells the reviewer where assistance entered and what the learner independently checked.

items.label: Name the assistance
items.detail: Identify tools and the tasks for which they were used.

items.label: Trace the evidence
items.detail: State which real sources, tests and outputs were checked.

items.label: Own the judgement
items.detail: Describe selection, revisions, decisions and individual or team contributions.

items.label: Follow the policy
items.detail: Keep assessment restrictions and rights boundaries intact.

sections.takeaway: Disclosure cannot legitimise fabricated evidence, prohibited tool use or missing permission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can test messages be sent to real recipients before the human checkpoint is proven?
checkpoint.answer: No. Test with destinations you control and demonstrate the checkpoint and failure path before any authorised external use.
